title: Post Office
strapline: Write it, stamp it, post it — and wait for the postie to bring one back.
intent: Nowhere gives mark-making a stronger purpose: a letter is writing that travels, and somebody real opens it at the other end.
Envelopes, addresses, stamps and postmarks surround children with print that does an actual job.
Sorting the post — by name, by size, by which room it's going to — is classification with a sack and a deadline.
Weighing parcels and counting out stamps and coins keeps honest maths at the counter.
The post office and the postie are part of children's own patch — people who help us, met on every street.
Folding letters, sticking stamps, sealing envelopes and franking the post are precise, satisfying hand-work.
implementation: Post things for real: cards to children's homes, a letter to the baby room, a parcel to the manager — a reply arriving transforms the play.
Model the writing purpose out loud: 'I'm writing to Grandma — Dear Grandma... Now it needs her address on the front so the postie knows where to go.'
Give every child a named pigeonhole or postbox so sorting the post means reading names — theirs and their friends'.
Set up the counter journey: queue, weigh the parcel, choose a stamp, pay, get it franked — each step is its own little job.
Add a balance scale and 'heavy parcel costs more' pricing so weighing has consequences.
Walk to the real post office or postbox to post something that genuinely matters — then wait together for the reply.
Take the customer role with problems: a parcel too big for the scales, a letter with no address — and let the postmaster solve it.
key_questions: Who is your letter for — and what do you want to tell them?
How will the postie know which house to take it to?
Is your parcel heavy or light? How many stamps will it need?
Whose name is on this envelope — which pigeonhole does it go in?
What happens to our letter after it disappears into the postbox?

impact.text: Children write letters, cards and parcels with real intended readers, and tell you exactly what their marks and letter-shapes say.
Children recognise their own name — and start to spot friends' names — as they sort post into the right pigeonholes.
Children sort the mail sack by size, shape and who it's for, and weigh parcels to decide which cost more to send.
Children count stamps onto envelopes and coins into the till, one by one, knowing the last number is the answer.
Children run counter scenes — queuing, serving, franking — that grow into sustained post office storylines with shared roles.
Children talk about the real postie, the postbox on their street and the post office as part of their own local patch.
Children wait their turn at the counter and take turns being the one with the franking stamp.
Children ask how the post actually works — where the van goes, how the letter finds the right house — and chase real answers.

enhancements: Real envelopes, sticky labels, old greetings cards and a shoulder mail sack.
Sticker 'stamps' priced 1p and 2p, and a date stamp with ink pad for franking.
Named pigeonholes photographed with each child's face beside their name.
A balance scale and parcels of honestly different weights (wrapped boxes with rice or foam inside).
A real postbox (or a convincing red one) that gets emptied ceremonially each day.
Addressed postcards home — every family primed to send a reply back to nursery.
A walk to the postbox to post real letters, timed for when the postie collects.

playing_exploring: Children investigate the whole hidden journey of a letter — writing it is only the beginning.
Envelopes, franking stamps and the mail sack invite hands-on exploration before any storyline starts.
active_learning: A letter begun must be written, sealed, stamped, posted and delivered — a long, satisfying chain children hold from end to end.
creating_thinking: Children invent who the post is from and what it says, and puzzle out real problems — the parcel with no address, the stamp that won't stick.
